posts.text:
The stack behind Nasab, and why each piece is there. 🧱

📱 Flutter: one codebase for iOS and Android. Riverpod (with codegen) for state, go_router for navigation, and a feature-first structure with three layers: domain, data, presentation. No use-case layer, because a solo dev doesn't need the ceremony.

🗄 Supabase Postgres: the family is the security boundary. Every family-scoped row is protected by row-level security, so you can read it only if you belong to that family. Privacy lives in the database, not in the UI.

⚡ 17 Supabase Edge Functions: push notifications fired from database events (a new memory, comment, like, tag or join), a daily reminders job, the subscription webhook and the storage proxy.

🖼 Firebase Storage for photos, video and voice. Uploads and downloads go through functions that check family membership first.

💳 RevenueCat for subscriptions. One plan per family, so only the owner pays.

📊 PostHog for product analytics. Every error toast in the app reports itself, so there's one choke point and no tracking calls scattered across screens.

The principle running through all of it: a family's archive should be private by default, enforced at the lowest layer possible.

What would you have done differently?

Designing one app for a grandmother and her teenage grandson is a fun constraint.

Most family apps look like either a genealogy database or a social feed. I wanted Nasab to feel like neither. It should feel like a keepsake book you'd find in a family cupboard.

A few decisions:
🎨 No tech blue. The palette is Heritage Brown, Antique Gold and Warm Ivory, taken from old albums and leather bindings.
🔤 Three typefaces with three jobs: Fraunces for names and headings, Lora Italic for anything emotional (quotes, captions), Inter for the UI.
✦ One motif, the 8-point star, used sparingly.
📚 Albums look like leather-bound covers with a gold emboss.
📳 Subtle haptics, and loading shimmers instead of spinners, so it feels calm, not busy.
🌍 Every screen works in Arabic, right to left.

The test I kept coming back to: would this look out of place in a grandparent's living room?

posts.text:
Nobody likes being the person who asks for the money back. 😬

So the "Remind" in Splitup isn't one button that nags. It's four voices, and you pick the one your friend deserves. 🎭

Splitup is an expense splitter for groups: trips, flats, dinners. The math is the easy part. The hard part is the message you send when someone owes you $39.16 and has gone quiet. 🫠

How the reminder works:
• 👆 From any settle-up suggestion, tap Remind and pick a tone: Friendly, Neutral, Firm or Rude.
• 🗂️ Each tone has its own pool of message templates (43 in total), so it never reads like a robot wrote it.
• ✍️ The name, amount and currency are filled in for you. You can regenerate the message, edit it, copy it or share it anywhere.
• 🔔 If the person is on Splitup, they get a notification too. It's limited to once an hour per group, so the app can't be used to spam anyone.

The decision I'm happiest with: Rude exists because friends are weird, but you choose it, you read it, and you send it. The app never decides to be mean on your behalf. 😤

A reminder that sounds like a bill collector costs you a friend. One that sounds like a joke gets you paid. 😄

The feature was never "send a notification". It was "make the awkward part optional".

This week I cut Nasab's prices in half, and added a Lifetime option. 🏷️

Heritage was $5.99 a month or $49.99 a year. It's now $2.99 and $24.99.

Why: I had priced it as if every family needed lots of storage from day one. They don't. Most families start small: a tree, birthdays, a few old photos, a voice note or two. The heavy storage comes later, as the archive grows over years. Charging for that up front was making people pay for space they weren't using yet.

So the price now matches how families actually start.

What changed:
💳 Monthly $2.99, yearly $24.99 (yearly is the best value)
🏛 New: Heritage Lifetime, $69.99 once. No renewals, one family, 20 GB of shared storage. A gift you can buy for your parents.
🗂 The 3-month plan is retired, so there are fewer choices to think about

The day Nasab went live, my backend stopped being only mine.

Old app builds stay installed for months. People update slowly, store review takes time, rollouts are staged. So at any moment, several versions of Nasab are talking to the same database.

That changed how I write every migration. These are the rules I work by now:

1. Additive schema only. New tables and nullable columns, never a rename or drop of something a shipped build reads.
2. Never change a function's signature. Add an optional parameter with a default, or ship fn_v2 and keep v1 alive.
3. Enum values can be added, never removed or renamed.
4. Security policies can't quietly revoke access an older build depends on.
5. If a change can't be backward compatible, it's a deliberate decision (a forced update or a deprecation window), never a side effect.

They sit at the very top of the project's engineering guide, above everything else.

118 migrations in, every one of them is forward-only.

For a family app this matters more than usual. The person on the oldest build is often the grandparent. They shouldn't be the one whose app breaks.

posts.text:
✈️ The hardest feature I've shipped in Splitup: adding an expense in airplane mode.

It sounds simple. Save it on the phone, upload it later. Then the edge cases show up:
• 🔁 the upload succeeds but the response is lost, so the app retries and creates a duplicate
• ✌️ two friends edit the same expense offline, on two phones
• 🗑️ someone deletes an expense while another phone is still offline
• 🕰️ older app versions, which know nothing about any of this, keep writing to the same database

What made it work: 🔧
1️⃣ Every expense gets an ID on the device (client_id). A unique index turns a retried upload into a no-op. Duplicates become impossible.
2️⃣ Every row has a version, bumped by the database on each update. An edit says which version it was based on, so conflicting offline edits get caught instead of silently overwriting each other.
3️⃣ Deletes leave a tombstone 🪦, so phones that were offline still learn the expense is gone.
4️⃣ The database stamps version and updated_at itself, with a trigger. Old builds, new builds and admin scripts all show up in the next sync without changing a line of their code.

⛴️ For the person on the ferry: they add the expense, the balance updates instantly, and it syncs when the signal comes back.

Offline-first is mostly about the unhappy paths. What's the nastiest sync bug you've met? 🐛

#Flutter #Supabase #BuildInPublic

posts.text:
For a while, every new signup on my app failed with "new row violates row-level security policy".

The policy was correct. The user's token was valid. And a plain insert of the exact same row worked.

Here's what was going on.

I'd added a small table to record which signup cohort a new user belonged to. Nothing in the app ever reads it, so I gave it an INSERT policy and no SELECT policy. Tight and minimal.

The client wrote to it with upsert(…, ignoreDuplicates: true), which Postgres runs as INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.

The catch: to resolve ON CONFLICT under row-level security, Postgres needs the row to be visible through a SELECT policy. Without one, the insert's check fails, even when no conflicting row exists.

The fix was one migration: a SELECT policy letting users see only their own row. That's safe, because they wrote every field in it.

The rule I've written down for myself: any RLS table written through upsert / ON CONFLICT needs a self-row SELECT policy, even if nothing ever selects from it.

It's also why I keep privacy in the database instead of the app. In Nasab, a family's photos and stories are protected by the same row-level rules. It just means those rules deserve their own tests.

Have you been bitten by an RLS edge case like this?

#Supabase #PostgreSQL #BuildInPublic

alt.summary: A code card showing an upsert with ignoreDuplicates failing with Postgres error 42501, and the fix: one SQL select policy that lets users read only their own row.

posts.title: The bug that broke every signup

The most important line in Nasab's daily reminders job isn't clever. It's this:

if (member.is_deceased) continue;

Nasab sends birthday and anniversary reminders to the whole family. Early on, I saw what the naive version would do: tell a family "Abba turns 81 tomorrow 🎉" a year after his funeral.

In a family app, a notification is never just a notification. It lands in someone's day.

So the reminders job (a scheduled Supabase Edge Function) is full of small kindnesses:
• It skips members who have passed away
• It skips dates the family only partly knows ("sometime in March 1950") instead of guessing
• It drops anniversaries of former spouses
• It handles Hijri birthdays, which shift about 11 days against the Gregorian calendar every year
• Tapping a reminder opens that person's celebration, not a generic home screen

None of these show up in a feature list. All of them show up in how the app feels.

What's an invisible detail you've shipped that users would only notice if it were missing?

Arabic has six plural forms. English has two. That's where localizing Nasab got interesting.

Nasab is built for families across South Asia, the Middle East and the diaspora, so Arabic was never an afterthought. Here's what shipping it took:

1️⃣ Centralise every string. All 1,000+ live in small per-feature ARB files, merged by a script, with a test that fails if the generated files drift.
2️⃣ Translate properly. Arabic plurals need zero, one, two, few, many and other forms. "3 members" and "11 members" take different word forms.
3️⃣ Respect gender. Many phrases change with the person's gender, so they're written as select cases.
4️⃣ Mirror the layout, deliberately. The whole UI flips right to left. The family tree canvas stays left to right on purpose.
5️⃣ Use real Arabic type. Markazi Text for headings, Noto Sans Arabic for body, Noto Naskh in place of italics.
6️⃣ Respect the calendar. Every date can show Hijri (Umm al-Qura or Misri) alongside Gregorian.
7️⃣ Meet people where they are. An Arabic-language phone opens Nasab in Arabic on first launch.

Localization isn't translation. It's making someone feel the app was built for them.

If you've shipped an RTL app: what surprised you most?

#Localization #Flutter #BuildInPublic

1/ The mobile rule nobody tells web devs: your old app versions never die. 📱 People update slowly. Store review adds lag. At any moment, five versions of your app are talking to one backend.

2/ So: add columns, never rename or drop ones a shipped build reads. New columns need a default or must be nullable.

3/ Need to change a function's signature? Don't. Ship fn_v2 and keep v1 alive until old builds age out.

4/ Enum values: add, never rename. And security rules must never revoke access an old build depends on.

$100 split three ways is $33.33, $33.33 and $33.33. That's $99.99. Where does the last cent go? 🪙

In an expense splitter this isn't trivia. If the shares don't add up to the bill, balances drift, settle-ups end at "you owe me 1 cent", and people stop trusting the numbers.

How Splitup handles money:
• 🔢 Amounts are stored as an integer number of cents, never as a decimal.
• ➗ Equal splits use integer division, then hand out the leftover cents one at a time. $100 becomes 3,334 + 3,333 + 3,333 cents. Always exactly $100.
• 🎯 Splits by percentage or by custom amount are rounded to the nearest cent, so they can be a cent off. That's why Splitup checks they add up before you can save, and does the same for multiple payers.
• 🧮 Balances are added up in cents. The settle-up step then works in dollars and ignores anything within a cent of zero.

Nobody sees any of this. They see "Your share: $33.34" and a settle-up that adds up.

Small rule, huge trust. 🤝 What's your money-handling rule? 👇

#MobileDev #Flutter #BuildInPublic

posts.text:
🧮 "Zero math" is Splitup's promise. Here's the math behind it.

Say Hitesh owes Max $40 for gas, and Max owes Ali $40 for dinner. The usual way: Hitesh pays Max, then Max pays Ali. Two payments, and Max is just a middleman.

🎯 In Splitup, Hitesh pays Ali $40. Max is settled automatically: he owes $40, he's owed $40, his balance is $0, so he isn't in any payment.

That works because Splitup settles on net balances, not on who owed whom:
1️⃣ Work out everyone's net balance: what they're owed minus what they owe.
2️⃣ Take the person who is owed the most and the person who owes the most.
3️⃣ The debtor pays the creditor the smaller of the two amounts. Repeat until every balance is within a cent.

On a real trip with 5 expenses and 3 people, that's the difference between 10 transfers and 2 payments.

It isn't guaranteed to find the absolute minimum number of payments for every possible group (that problem gets hard fast). But it's fast, easy to explain, and real friend groups usually land close to the minimum.

🤝 Then the product takes over: Settle records the payment, Remind sends a nudge, Share sends the whole plan to the group chat.

Do you optimize for perfect, or for explainable? 👇

#Algorithms #BuildInPublic #ProductDesign

posts.text:
Nasab went from first commit to "Phase 16 done" in 5 days. 🚀

Not because AI is magic. Because the plan was the prompt.

Before writing any code I wrote a spec: scope, database schema, security rules, and a build plan split into numbered phases. Every phase ends with an acceptance checklist.

Then the loop:
1️⃣ Claude Code builds one phase.
2️⃣ I test it against that phase's checklist.
3️⃣ If a box doesn't tick, the phase isn't done, however good the code looks.
4️⃣ Commit. Next phase.

The commit log:
Jul 18: Phase 0 and 1
Jul 21: up to Phase 9, then FCM push notifications
Jul 22: Phase 16 done

The most useful section of the spec? "Out of scope." AI features, OCR, GEDCOM export, offline mode, payments, dark mode. Written down, so neither of us wandered.

To be clear: Phase 16 was not launch. Then came weeks of real work: a rewritten tree layout engine, voice notes, sign-in, store builds. 160+ commits so far.

Some of my users' birthdays move about 11 days every year.

The Hijri (Islamic) calendar is lunar, with a year of roughly 354 days. Families who mark birthdays and anniversaries by it see the Gregorian date slide earlier each year. Over about 33 years, a Hijri birthday travels all the way around the Gregorian calendar.

Building for that taught me a few things:

• There isn't one Hijri calendar. Nasab supports Umm al-Qura and the Misri calendar, and each family chooses.
• Date pickers need a toggle, because some dates are only known in Hijri.
• Reminders can't be computed once. The Hijri date has to be resolved again every year.
• Partial dates are real. "Muharram 1385" with no day is a valid memory, but not a valid reminder.
• Show both. In Nasab every date can display Hijri next to Gregorian, because many families live in both calendars at once.

Calendars encode culture. Getting them right says "we built this for you" louder than any marketing copy.

Have you ever had to support a non-Gregorian calendar?

posts.text:
The worst bugs don't crash. They make it look like nothing happened.

In Nasab, after you joined a family, the app was supposed to move you on to the next onboarding screen. Sometimes it just… didn't. Relaunch the app and everything was fine.

The cause was Riverpod auto-dispose.

The controller behind that step existed only to run one method, and nothing was watching it. The method awaited a write to local storage, then invalidated another provider.

During that await, Riverpod saw a provider with zero listeners and disposed it. The next line touched a disposed ref and threw, and an error handler upstream swallowed the exception. No crash, no toast, just a redirect that never happened.

The fix is a tiny extension that holds a keepAlive link for the duration of the call: ref.keepingAlive(() async { … }).

Then I audited every controller with the same shape (an await followed by a ref call, with no listeners) and applied the fix to ten more.

Lesson: in reactive frameworks, "who keeps this alive?" matters as much as "what does this do?"

#Flutter #Riverpod #BuildInPublic

Add a friend to your group before they download the app, and they end up in it twice. Here's how I fixed that in Splitup. 👻

An admin can add people by name and start logging expenses straight away. Those are "ghost" members. When the real person joined with the invite code, the app created a brand-new member for them, and their share of every past expense stayed with the ghost.

The fix, shipped without breaking a single older app version:
• 🧱 A new column, is_claimed, set by a database trigger that checks the member against real accounts. It never trusts what the app sends.
• 🙋 Right after someone joins, if the group has ghosts, a sheet asks: "Is one of these you?"
• 🔀 Confirming calls one database function that moves the ghost's history (who paid, who owes, reminders) onto the real account and removes the duplicate. The identity comes from the session on the server, so nobody can claim as someone else.
• 🔐 The ghost row is locked during the claim, so two people tapping the same name at once can't both win.
• ⏭️ "Skip, I'm new" makes no call at all. The safest default is doing nothing.

For users: add friends today, and they claim their spot whenever they finally install it.

For a while, some Splitup purchases were credited twice. Here's how that happens, and how I fixed it. 🐞

Splitup sells one-time group packs. Buy a pack and your group allowance goes up. The original flow lived in the app: after a purchase, the app inserted a row, a database trigger fired, and a function raised the allowance.

Then I added a RevenueCat webhook, server to server, so purchases get granted even if the app crashes mid-flow or the user is on an old build.

Two paths, one purchase. 🔀 Their de-duplication keys didn't reliably match, so the same purchase could be granted by both.

The fix:
1️⃣ One source of truth. The webhook calls a single database function that records the purchase and raises the allowance in one atomic step.
2️⃣ The store's transaction ID gets a unique index, so a redelivered webhook can't grant twice.
3️⃣ The old app-side trigger is disabled. The app no longer writes purchases at all; it just watches the allowance update in real time.

💡 Lesson: the moment you add a second path to the same side effect, you have a distributed systems problem. Pick one owner.

Ever had two code paths fighting over the same row? 👇

#Payments #Supabase #BuildInPublic

posts.text:
Airplane mode is my favourite tester. ✈️

Users are offline far more than founders expect: on trips, in basements, in lifts, on flights. Two of my apps, Splitup and My Deen, work without signal. Here's what that takes:

1. Write locally first. The tap updates the screen instantly, the server finds out later.

2. Queue the change and say so. Splitup shows "2 changes waiting to sync" so nobody wonders where their expense went.

3. Never make a tap wait for the server. I learned this the hard way: a loading spinner in My Deen that could spin forever with no signal.

4. Decide what wins when two phones disagree. Before it happens, not after.

5. Test sync without a network. Splitup's test suite runs against an in-memory sync server, so I can break the connection on purpose, every time.

Offline-first costs more on day one. It saves you every one-star review that starts with "I lost my data."

Does your app survive airplane mode?

I planned 30 days of Instagram and LinkedIn content for Nasab in one working session with Claude Opus 5.5. Here's how it worked, and where I had to step in.

1️⃣ Feed it real material, not a brief.
It read Nasab's own docs, the App Store screenshot kit, the release notes, my founder's note and the landing page. That's why the posts talk about Hijri reminders, Send a Wish and Scan Photo instead of generic "family app" copy.

2️⃣ Ask for a system, not posts.
One prompt gave me a design system for Instagram, a "Build Log" variant for LinkedIn, hook formulas and 34 post specs (21 Instagram, 13 LinkedIn). Each has on-image copy, a caption, hashtags and alt text.

3️⃣ Make the images code.
Every image is an HTML page rendered by one script, reusing the kit behind my App Store screenshots. Change a headline, re-run, done.

4️⃣ Build the thing you'll actually post from.
The calendar in the image is generated from the post specs. Every post expands into its caption, hashtags and alt text with a copy button.

5️⃣ Steer hard.
I dropped the post numbering, moved from square to 4:5 and banned em dashes. It turned that last rule into a check that blocks rendering if a dash slips in.

⭐ I only ask for an App Store review when nobody owes anybody anything.

Review prompts are rare. iOS shows the sheet about three times a year, and Android has its own quota. Spend one at a bad moment and you get a one-star review from someone mid-argument about $39.16.

So Splitup's review policy is a small, unit-tested piece of pure Dart. A prompt can only fire on a happy moment:
• 🤝 right after you settle a suggested payment
• ✅ when a settlement leaves the whole group owing nothing
• 💸 after you record a payment
• 🎯 when you hit your 5th, 15th or 40th expense

And never when: 🚫
• 🗓️ you've had the app for less than 3 days
• 🧭 you haven't done at least 3 meaningful things yet
• ⏳ you were asked in the last 90 days, or 3 times already
• 📝 you rated the app yourself in the last 180 days
• 💳 you saw the paywall this session

Every skipped prompt logs a reason, so I can see which rule does the work.

Timing is part of the product. ⏱️ When does your app ask for a review? 👇

AI wrote my iOS TestFlight pipeline in one pull request. Getting it green took 10 more commits. Same day. 😅

The pipeline: Fastlane plus GitHub Actions, so every merge puts a fresh build of Nasab on testers' phones.

Claude Code wrote the whole thing on its own branch. Lanes, workflow, secrets. It looked right. It was about 90% right.

The other 10%, in order of discovery:
• Code signing hung forever. Fix: a temporary keychain created just for CI.
• An empty BUILD_NUMBER variable silently skipped the fallback.
• Apple Generic Versioning had to be switched on, twice (app and tests).
• The runner needed macOS 15 and the newest Xcode available.
• A Flutter Swift Package Manager bug needed a workaround.
• One xcodebuild step just needed a longer timeout.

None of this is in the docs the AI learned from. It's in today's runner image, my certificates, my project file.

That's the honest shape of AI-assisted development: it gets you to the hard part much faster. The hard part is still yours.

Docs are the map. CI is the territory.

🎨 I redesigned splitup.tappstudio.in with Claude Opus 5.5. The part that mattered most wasn't the layout. It was the rules the page had to follow.

A landing page for an expense splitter has one job: say "Split. Remind. Settle." in three seconds, then get out of the way. Here is what we held it to:

• 🎯 One source of truth for the look. Colours, radii and spacing are mirrored from the Flutter app's own tokens. The rule in the README: change a colour in the app first, then port it here. Never invent one. So the site, the store screenshots and the app read as one product.
• 🧰 No build step. Plain HTML and CSS, no node_modules, nothing to install. Open index.html and it works.
• 📱 The hero phone isn't a screenshot. It's a live HTML port of the app's UI at true app scale, and it switches to the app's dark theme when the page does.
• 🌗 Light and dark mode with a toggle and no flash on load. Per-theme values are tokens, so a component never needs its own dark rule.
• 🪶 Small on purpose. Inline SVG icons instead of a 323 KB icon font. Ten gallery screenshots cut from 2.7 MB to under 700 KB as WebP. Poppins self-hosted.
• ✍️ Copy rules too: no em dashes anywhere, and the pricing is stated plainly: create 1 group free, join unlimited, one-time packs after that.

💡 What I'd tell anyone designing with an AI model: write the rules down in the README before the second prompt. A written rule survives every new session. So do the lessons. A clipped hero headline and chips that vanished in dark mode are both documented there now, with the fix.

The model gave me speed. ⚡ The README gave me consistency. 📖

What rule would you write down first? 👇
